name: Avianus
credit: Avianus, Fables: the fox and the dog (Latin manuscript of the 10th century; Bibliothèque nationale de France, NAL 1132, fol. 39) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Avianus is a Latin writer of fables who flourished around the end of the fourth century or the beginning of the fifth. Almost nothing is known of his life: his name is also met as Avienus, and he must not be confused with Rufius Festus Avienus, the translator of Aratus. His one surviving work is a collection of forty-two fables in elegiac couplets, introduced by a prose letter of dedication to a certain Theodosius, whom many scholars take to be Macrobius Ambrosius Theodosius.

The fables turn the stock tales of the Aesopic tradition, among them the tortoise and the eagle, the north wind and the sun, the crow and the pitcher, into polished Latin verse, each ending in a brief moral. The collection became one of the most widely read school texts of the Middle Ages, was copied, imitated and rewritten in verse and prose many times, and fed directly into the later European fable literature. The text here follows the edition of Robinson Ellis (Oxford, 1887).
